Metatorbernite is the copper uranyl phosphate mineral Cu(UO2)2(PO4)2(H2O)4·4H2O in the September 2026 IMA list, with grandfathered status G. The year 1916 is a historical description year, not a numbered IMA approval. Its ideal eight-water composition is distinct from twelve-water torbernite, arsenate metazeunerite, calcium meta-autunite, uranyl ions and elemental uranium or copper. Locock and Burns grew synthetic metatorbernite in copper-bearing silica gel at room temperature over three weeks and refined an epoxy-coated, merohedrally twinned crystal in P4/n. Its 88.3(6)% fitted copper-site occupancy and constrained hydrogen model are specimen-specific; proposed oxonium charge compensation was not directly established. The 2023 natural Cornwall crystal instead gave the preferred P4/nmm model with a smaller c repeat. These are source-specific structural models, not grounds to replace all specimens with one symmetry or transfer occupancy between them. Thermal behavior below is abiotic laboratory evidence; neither criticality nor microbial extraction, isolated-product recovery or industrial deployment is inferred.

Metazeunerite is the copper uranyl arsenate mineral Cu(UO2)2(AsO4)2(H2O)4·4H2O in the September 2026 IMA list, with grandfathered status G. The year 1937 is a historical description year, not a numbered IMA approval. Its ideal eight-water composition is distinct from twelve-water zeunerite, phosphate metatorbernite, calcium meta-autunite and elemental uranium, arsenic or copper. Locock and Burns synthesized its analogue hydrothermally at 220(1) degrees C for 24 h after controlled heating, then refined an epoxy-coated, twinned crystal in P4/n at room temperature. The hydrogen model was constrained; metatorbernite copper deficiency is not a metazeunerite result. A later natural German specimen gave a preferred P4/nmm model with a smaller c repeat, while synthetic low-temperature powder data were indexed orthorhombically. These specimen- and condition-specific models are preserved rather than merged. The thermal evidence is laboratory and abiotic; no criticality, microbial mechanism, isolated-product recovery or industrial deployment is inherited from composition.
The hydrogen refinement constrained O-H lengths to approximately 0.96 angstrom and fixed displacement parameters.
CISTI observed and calculated structure factors remain unacquired.
The two rechecked 2004 errata concern other articles, not a demonstrated correction of the 2003 paper.

source_assessments.decision: curate separately qualified natural thermal arms
limits: Sections 3.2 and 4 and Figure 4 report diffraction changes attributed to dehydration at approximately 353, 373 and 483 K for natural sample 1 in air, with strongest expansion normal to its autunite-type layers. Table 1 and Section 2.3 support the P4/nmm refinement of this natural crystal; the authors explicitly tested alternative models and did not obtain an equivalent satisfactory P4/n refinement. The geometric thermal-expansion fits and powder patterns are complementary measurements, not independent metal-recovery trials.

The extra transitions in mixtures of pristine and partly dehydrated metatorbernite are given as 313 and 463 K in Section 3.2 but 303 and 473 K in Section 4; neither pair is adopted as a corrected threshold. The article does not provide a matched water mass balance for these diffraction arms, and instability can begin during handling or irradiation. Its fitted bond-length changes and proposed interlayer explanation do not identify every dehydration product. The cited crystallographic deposits remain unacquired, so no independent re-refinement is claimed.

Table 1 and Sections 2.3 and 3.2 support P4/nmm for natural crystal 2a at 100 K and strongly anisotropic thermal expansion. Section 3.2 and Figure 5 report powder diffraction changes at approximately 283 and 543 K in vacuum, interpreted as two dehydration steps, and a separate 100-333 K experiment reaching a partially dehydrated state. These are source-assigned events for the specified natural material, not fixed species-wide decomposition temperatures or a metal extraction result.

Figure 5c-d caption incorrectly calls its material metatorbernite while the figure introduction, equations and surrounding text refer to metazeunerite, sample 2. The 93 K plotted start differs from the 100 K method boundary; no precise 2a/2b assignment is supplied for Figure 5. The study does not directly measure the water content of each intermediate by a paired mass-loss assay; its suggested greater flexibility of the arsenate layer and delayed water loss remain a structural interpretation. The cited CSD/ICSD files remain unacquired, precluding independent diffraction re-refinement.

source_assessments.decision: Curate separately scoped synthetic thermal observations and preserve inconsistent temperature wording.
limits: Section 3 and Figure 4 show the synthetic phosphate end member retaining tetragonal indexing on cooling, expanding anisotropically on heating, and developing a high-temperature amorphous signature followed by an unidentified crystalline product on cooling. The source distinguishes this sealed-capillary behavior from earlier natural specimens heated in open systems. Its room-temperature synthetic solid-solution series supports phosphate-arsenate substitution as another experimental variable; it does not prove all natural samples are pure end members.

Figure S5 displays distinct synthetic metatorbernite traces through 423 K, a largely diffuse 473 K trace, and a changed 293 K trace after cooling; S6 shows departure from the preceding a/c trend above approximately 373 K. These figures support the qualitative sequence, without assigning a sharp transition temperature from coarse sampling.

The abstract places amorphization at 473 K, Results says greater than 473 K, a later discussion says greater than 423 K, and Conclusion says above 373 K. Those wordings are retained as inconsistent bounds, not combined into one precise threshold; S5 distinguishes the plotted 423 and 473 K states. The study does not directly establish water stoichiometry at every temperature, and the high-temperature and cooled products are not completely identified. Its natural spoil compositions were inferred from a synthetic lattice-parameter calibration after 80-degree-C drying; they are not direct assays of untreated in-situ hydration or mineral-specific uranium retention.

Section 3 and Figure 5 describe the synthetic arsenate end member as tetragonal initially, orthorhombic on cooling to 110 K, mixed orthorhombic/tetragonal at 293 K during reheating, and tetragonal again at 323 K. The authors call the orthorhombic indexing preliminary and identify the high-temperature product as unknown. This observed synthetic sequence differs from the 2023 natural-crystal model and vacuum powder behavior, rather than independently confirming their exact transition temperatures.

Figure S9 gives the synthetic arsenate end-member cooling/heating sequence, including the 110 K, 293 K reheating, 323 K, 373 K, 423 K, 473 K and final cooled 293 K patterns. S7 and S8 instead belong to the mixed phosphate-arsenate composition and are not assigned to pure metazeunerite.

The abstract places the new high-temperature phase at 473 K, Results says above 373 K, and the later comparison says 150 degrees C (about 423 K); Figure S9 provides sampled states rather than a unique transition onset. The paper also prints an arsenate-only formula in a sentence calling the composition mixed phosphate-arsenate. Neither that wording nor the mixed-member transition is used as an end-member measurement. Water content at each temperature, the high-temperature product and the causal origin of the low-temperature symmetry change remain unresolved. No quantitative uranium or arsenic recovery, microbial causality or durable field immobilization is demonstrated.
The article statement that all prior structural studies used natural material is overbroad: Locock and Burns 2003 used synthetic crystals. This statement is not adopted.
Figshare metadata labels the supplement CC BY 4.0, while its embedded footer says CC BY 3.0. Both are retained; the raw file stays outside Git.

limits: Natural Trapelia involuta on heterogeneous South Terras substrates is a field observation, not an axenic controlled experiment.
Page 161 reports hyphae contacting and occasionally penetrating cleavage in metatorbernite and metazeunerite, with no observed dissolution etch pits or rounding.
The control was from a separate Scottish site near Palnackie. Field material was air-dried, with no controlled incubation time, pH or mineral loading.
EMPA values are background and three-standard-deviation adjusted counts, not calibrated mass concentrations. Fifty spots along a 180-micrometre traverse are not fifty biological replicates.
Localized U, Cu and Fe and histochemical evidence support a proposed melanin-like association. No isolated-metal product, exact-mineral mass balance or molecular causal test is reported.
NCBI Taxonomy EFetch 91807 verifies Trapelia involuta at species rank but does not authenticate the field specimens or identify the photobiont.
The 1998 McLean correspondence is a related preliminary study. The 2003 proceedings lead and 2004 follow-up must not automatically be counted as independent replications.
